d.chapter: Economic Geography — Natural Regions: 3. Desert Regions
d.notions: Desert, hot desert, cold desert, erg, reg, hamada, trade winds, cold ocean current, rain shadow.
d.focus: Location and types of deserts; general characteristics and causes of deserts.
d.competence: Learners are able to find the deserts of the world on a map and explain why the Sahara, north of Cameroon, is so dry.
objectives: Locate the main deserts of the world.
Distinguish between hot and cold deserts, and between sandy, stony and rocky deserts.
recall: The Tropical Grassland lies between 5° and 15° north and south of the Equator.
Its drier part, the Sahel, is threatened by desertification.
North of the Sahel lies the largest hot desert in the world.
d.recallNote: Check the homework: three countries covered by the Sahara.
situation: In Garoua, Salma watches a documentary about the Sahara. She is surprised to see that it is not only sand: there are also plains covered with stones and bare rocky mountains.
She had always thought that a desert was only a sea of sand dunes.
sitQA: What is the problem raised in the situation above?
The problem is that Salma thought that a desert was only sand, but she discovers that deserts can also be stony or rocky.
What three kinds of surface did Salma see in the documentary?
She saw sand dunes, plains covered with stones and bare rocky mountains.
How can Salma learn more about the different types of deserts?
She can study maps and pictures in her atlas and textbook, and ask her geography teacher.
d.justification: This lesson will help us to know where the deserts of the world are found, their types, and why they are so dry.

qa.q: A region receives less than 250 mm of rain per year and has very little vegetation. What do we call it?
qa.a: Such a region is called a desert.

qa.q: Find the main deserts on the map.
Look at the map. Near which lines of latitude are most hot deserts found?
qa.a: Most hot deserts are found near the Tropic of Cancer and the Tropic of Capricorn, between about 15° and 30° north and south of the Equator.

qa.q: Look at the map. On which side of the continents are most hot deserts found: east or west?
qa.a: Most hot deserts are found on the western side of the continents, for example the Sahara, the Namib, the Atacama and the Great Australian Desert.

sum.title: I. Definition and Location
defs: A desert is a region that receives less than 250 mm of rain per year and has very little vegetation.
sum.intro: Hot deserts are found between about 15° and 30° north and south of the Equator, mostly on the western sides of continents. The main ones are the following:
items: A. In Africa
The Sahara in North Africa, the largest hot desert in the world, and the Kalahari and the Namib in Southern Africa.
deserts_world.png
B. In Asia
The Arabian Desert and the Thar Desert in India and Pakistan.
C. In America and Australia
The Sonoran and Mojave Deserts in North America, the Atacama in South America, and the Great Australian Desert.

qa.q: The Gobi Desert in Asia is dry, but its winters are very cold. What type of desert is it?
qa.a: The Gobi is a cold desert, also called a mid-latitude desert. The Sahara is a hot desert.

qa.q: In the Sahara, some areas are seas of sand, some are stony plains and some are bare rock. What are these three surfaces called?
qa.a: A sandy desert is called an erg, a stony desert is called a reg, and a rocky desert is called a hamada.

sum.title: II. Types of Deserts
sum.intro: Deserts can be classified according to their temperature and according to their surface:
items: A. According to Temperature
Hot deserts, like the Sahara, are hot all year. Cold deserts, like the Gobi, have very cold winters.
B. According to Surface
– An erg is a sandy desert with dunes.
– A reg is a stony desert.
– A hamada is a rocky desert.

qa.q: The trade winds that blow over the Sahara come from the land, not from the sea. Why do they bring no rain?
qa.a: They bring no rain because they blow over land and are dry. They also get warmer as they move towards the Equator, so they do not form clouds.

qa.q: The Namib Desert lies along the coast, next to the cold Benguela current. How does this cold current make the coast dry?
qa.a: The cold current cools the air above it. Cool air cannot rise and form rain clouds, so it gives only fog and no rain.

sum.title: III. Causes of Deserts
sum.intro: The main causes of deserts are the following:
items: A. Dry Trade Winds
The trade winds blow from the land. They are dry and bring no rain.
B. Cold Ocean Currents
Cold currents cool the air, so it cannot form rain clouds. Examples: the Benguela current (Namib) and the Humboldt current (Atacama).
C. Distance from the Sea
The centres of large continents are far from the sea, so moist winds do not reach them, as in the Gobi.
D. Rain Shadow
Mountains stop moist winds, so the land behind them is dry, as in Patagonia.

evaluation: Why are most hot deserts found on the western sides of the continents?
They are found there because of dry trade winds blowing from the land and cold ocean currents along the coasts.
What is the difference between an erg and a reg?
An erg is a sandy desert with dunes, while a reg is a stony desert.
Name one hot desert and one cold desert.
The Sahara is a hot desert and the Gobi is a cold desert.
remediation: A desert receives less than ______ mm of rain per year.
The largest hot desert in the world is the ______.
A sandy desert is called an ______.
A stony desert is called a ______, and a rocky desert is called a ______.
The cold current along the Namib Desert is the ______ current.
The Gobi is an example of a ______ desert.
d.remediationAnswers: 1. 250 2. Sahara 3. erg 4. reg, hamada 5. Benguela 6. cold
d.homework: Think about the hottest days of March in Garoua. Are the nights also very hot, or cooler? Write two sentences about the difference between day and night.
d.homeworkTag: This prepares Part 2: The Climate of Hot Deserts.
